DOCUMENT:
2026 Employee Engagement Survey: Results Report
People Analytics Team, Brightwell Housing Association, April 2026

1. Summary
The 2026 engagement survey ran from 2 to 20 March and 1,150 colleagues responded. The overall engagement index rose from 65 to 68, its highest level since the survey began in 2019. This report sets out results by division and theme and recommends priorities for 2026-27.

2. Method
All 1,980 employees on the payroll on 1 March were invited by email, with paper questionnaires and protected time offered to repairs operatives without regular computer access. The survey was administered by an external provider and was confidential: no results are reported for groups of fewer than ten respondents. The engagement index is the mean of six questions on pride, advocacy, intention to stay, motivation, discretionary effort and satisfaction, scaled to 0-100. The questions are unchanged from 2025, so year-on-year comparisons are like for like.

3. Response and engagement by division
Table 1. Response rates and engagement index by division
Division | Headcount 2026 | Responses 2026 | Response rate 2026 | Response rate 2025 | Engagement 2025 | Engagement 2026
Repairs and Maintenance | 820 | 254 | 31% | 64% | 58 | 63
Housing Management | 610 | 427 | 70% | 78% | 69 | 70
Customer Services | 340 | 228 | 67% | 74% | 66 | 68
Central Services | 210 | 141 | 67% | 81% | 72 | 71
Total | 1,980 | 1,050 | 53% | 72% | 65 | 68

The overall response rate fell from 72% to 53%, which remains above the 50% benchmark our provider regards as robust for organisations of our size.

Every division improved its engagement score this year. The largest gain was in Repairs and Maintenance, up five points to 63. Repairs has historically been our least engaged division, and in 2025 it was the focus of a major programme: new vans and tablets for all operatives, a revised bonus scheme and monthly team briefings led by the Director of Property. The results suggest this investment is paying off.

4. Results by theme
Table 2. Theme scores (percentage agreeing), organisation-wide
Theme | 2025 | 2026 | Change
My manager supports my development | 61% | 66% | +5
I have the tools to do my job well | 54% | 62% | +8
I understand the organisation's priorities | 70% | 72% | +2
Workload is manageable | 49% | 47% | -2
I would recommend Brightwell as a place to work | 58% | 63% | +5

Tools and equipment showed the biggest improvement of any theme, consistent with the investment in Repairs. Workload remains the weakest area and is the only theme to decline. Free-text comments on workload most often referred to vacancy cover in Housing Management, where 41 posts were vacant at the time of the survey.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Extend the Repairs model of regular director-led briefings to Housing Management and Customer Services in 2026-27, given the improvement it has delivered in Repairs.
5.2 Prioritise recruitment to Housing Management vacancies, with a target to halve the vacancy count by October.
5.3 Repeat the survey in March 2027 with the same questions and method.

6. Conclusion
2026 shows real and broad-based progress. Engagement is at its highest level since 2019, every division improved, and the division where we invested most improved most. The Executive Team can be confident that the 2025 engagement programme worked, and should extend its most effective elements across the organisation.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "The 2026 engagement survey ran from 2 to 20 March and 1,150 colleagues responded." -- The summary says 1,150 colleagues responded, but Table 1 totals 1,050 responses (254 + 427 + 228 + 141), which is also the figure consistent with the stated 53% response rate (1,050/1,980).
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Every division improved its engagement score this year." -- Table 1 shows Central Services fell from 72 to 71. Not every division improved; the claim is repeated in the conclusion.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "The largest gain was in Repairs and Maintenance, up five points to 63." -- Table 1 shows the Repairs response rate halved from 64% to 31%. With fewer than a third of Repairs staff responding, the rise could reflect who responded (e.g. disengaged staff opting out) rather than a real improvement. The report never addresses non-response bias, yet the conclusion that the Repairs programme 'worked' and should be extended depends on that division's result.

REVIEW:
# Review: 2026 Employee Engagement Survey Results Report

**The recommendation is clear, but the document is not ready for the Executive Team.** Two headline claims are contradicted by the report's own tables, and the main conclusion (the Repairs programme worked, so extend it) rests on a result that the response data undermine.

## Factual errors to fix before circulation

**1. The respondent count is wrong in the Summary.** The Summary says 1,150 colleagues responded. Table 1 sums to **1,050** (254 + 427 + 228 + 141). 1,050 / 1,980 is the 53% reported. Your own description ("more than 1,100") repeats the wrong figure. Someone on the Executive Team who adds up the table will find this.

**2. "Every division improved" is false.** Central Services fell from **72 to 71**. The Summary doesn't say it, but Section 3 and the Conclusion both do. One point is probably noise, but the claim as written is wrong. Change it to "three of four divisions improved; Central Services was broadly stable."

## The central problem: Repairs response rate halved

The Repairs response rate fell from **64% to 31%**, even with paper copies and protected time. The report mentions the overall drop (72% → 53%) but not this one, and this one matters most.

- **The 50% benchmark is cleared overall but missed badly in Repairs.** Repairs is the division the conclusion depends on, and at 31% it has the least robust result in the report.
- **Non-response bias can explain the +5 without any real change.** About 525 Repairs colleagues responded in 2025 and 254 in 2026. If disengaged operatives were the ones who stopped responding, the average would rise even if nobody's views changed. A survey cannot tell "engagement rose" apart from "the less engaged stopped answering" when half the respondents disappear.
- **The collapse is itself a warning sign.** A sharp fall in participation in the division you invested in most could mean survey fatigue, distrust of confidentiality, or disengagement. It needs explaining, not leaving out.

**It also inflates the overall figure.** Repairs is the lowest-scoring division, and its share of respondents fell from about 37% to 24%. Using the 2025 response mix (and assuming similar 2025 headcounts), the 2026 index comes out at about **67.2 rather than 68**. So roughly a quarter of the headline gain comes from *who* responded, not from changed views. Weighting by headcount gives about 64.2 → 66.9. Either way the gain is real but smaller, and the report should present a weighted figure or at least note this.

## Attribution claims go beyond the evidence

- **Tools and equipment (+8) is organisation-wide.** Table 2 gives no divisional breakdown, so the report cannot show the gain came from Repairs. With Repairs a *smaller* share of respondents this year, the gain may be mostly elsewhere. Add a Repairs-only theme breakdown. If it shows a large tools gain in Repairs, the argument gets much stronger.
- **Recommendation 5.1 picks one element without evidence.** The 2025 programme had three parts: vans and tablets, a revised bonus scheme, and director-led briefings. The report offers no evidence that the briefings drove any improvement. The tools data, if anything, points to equipment. Extending briefings "given the improvement it has delivered" is not supported. Either give evidence specific to briefings (for example, a manager or communication item in Repairs) or reword it as a pilot.
- **Workload and Housing Management vacancies.** The link is reasonable, and the 41 vacancies are a concrete figure. But free-text comments come from a self-selected subset, and Housing Management's overall engagement actually rose (69 → 70). Present this as "comments suggest" rather than as an established cause. Recommendation 5.2 still stands on its own merits.

## Smaller points

- **No margins of error.** Changes of 1 to 2 points (Housing Management +1, Central Services −1, priorities +2, workload −2) are probably within noise, especially at lower response rates. Say so, so the Executive Team doesn't read signal into them.
- **"Highest since the survey began in 2019"** is not backed by any figures in the report. Add a short trend line or footnote.
- **The method section says comparisons are "like for like."** The questions are, but the respondent population isn't. Qualify this.
- **Recommendation 5.3 should add a response-rate action for Repairs.** Find out why participation collapsed and set a target, or the 2027 comparison will have the same weakness.

## Suggested rewording of the Conclusion

> Engagement rose from 65 to 68 (about 67 after adjusting for the changed response mix), with gains in three of four divisions. Repairs and Maintenance, the focus of 2025 investment, recorded the largest increase (58 → 63). However, its response rate halved to 31%, so this result should be treated with caution. We recommend prioritising Housing Management recruitment, piloting director-led briefings in one further division alongside a Repairs-specific analysis of which programme elements made a difference, and investigating the fall in Repairs participation before the 2027 survey.

## Bottom line

The story may well be positive, and the effort to reach operatives without computer access is creditable. As written, though, the report contains two checkable errors and leaves out the one fact (the Repairs response collapse) most likely to be raised in the room. Fixing these makes the report more credible to the Executive Team, not less.
